opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people frame it as a religious question, humanoid or not, but I see it more as a question about where you believe the bottleneck is.

The strongest argument for humanoids isn't really that the human form is optimal. It's that the world is already built around it: doorknobs, stairs, shelves, tools, car interiors, factory stations. And maybe even more importantly, the data is built around it. If you believe the path to general-purpose robots runs through learning from huge amounts of human video and teleoperation, then a body that roughly matches human kinematics makes that transfer much easier. You can map a person's hand motion onto a robot hand more directly. So the humanoid bet is really a bet on generality and on data.

The non-humanoid camp says: fine, but look at what actually ships and makes money today. Wheeled bases with one or two arms, simple grippers, no legs. That's cheaper, more reliable, easier to keep safe, and in most warehouses and factories the floor is flat, so legs add cost and failure modes without adding much value. Their bet is that you can get to useful deployment sooner, collect real-world data from robots that are actually working, and let the intelligence improve on a platform that's commercially viable now.

My own view is that the hardware form is downstream of the model question. Right now no one has a robot brain that's truly general, so the body that gets deployed is often the one whose limitations matter least for a narrow task. If the foundation models get much better at generalizing, the value of a general body goes up a lot, and humanoids start to make more economic sense. If progress stays task-specific for longer, the pragmatic forms win the near term.

There's also an honest point about capital and narrative. Humanoids are much easier to raise money for. They're visually compelling, and investors understand the dream immediately. That's not a criticism by itself, but it means some of the humanoid wave is driven by financing dynamics, not just technical conviction. The companies that survive will be the ones that can turn the demo into reliable hours of work at a cost per hour that beats the alternative.

So I'd say both bets are rational, but they're bets on different timelines. Non-humanoid is a bet on the next three to five years of deployment. Humanoid is a bet that the general-purpose robot arrives, and that when it does, the form that fits our world and our data wins. And I wouldn't be surprised if the answer ends up being somewhere in between: humanoid upper bodies with dexterous hands on wheeled bases, because hands and manipulation are where generality really matters, and legs are often the most expensive part to justify.

r001.rationale: It contrasts legged humanoids with wheeled platforms and notes that legs add cost, but does not suggest leg presence is the main hardware difference between the companies.

r002.rationale: It presents the argument that the world is already built around the human form and says that a body matching it fits our world, making humanoids a natural fit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the humanoid versus non-humanoid framing is a bit of a false binary, and it hides what the actual bet is.

The argument for humanoids is pretty simple on the surface: the world is built for humans. Doorknobs, stairs, shelves, tools, factory lines—everything is shaped around a body of a certain height with two arms and two legs. So if you build a general-purpose robot, the human form is the "universal adapter." You don't have to redesign the environment. And there's a second, more subtle argument, which is about data. If your robot has roughly human morphology, then human video—teleoperation, motion capture, even just YouTube—becomes a much more direct source of training signal. The embodiment gap is smaller.

The argument against is also simple: humanoids are hard. Bipedal balance burns a lot of energy and engineering effort on a problem that wheels solved a century ago. Five-fingered hands are expensive and fragile. You're paying a huge complexity tax to look like a person, when a wheeled base with two arms would do ninety percent of the work in a warehouse for a fraction of the cost. Companies like Agility ended up with legs but not quite a human form, and a lot of the actual deployed robots in logistics look nothing like people.

So where do I land? I think the real question isn't "humanoid or not," it's "what are you betting is the bottleneck?" If you believe the bottleneck is intelligence—that once the model is good enough, hardware will be commoditized—then you want the most general body possible, because the model will be what differentiates you, and a general body means a bigger market. That's the humanoid bet, and it's really a bet on foundation models for robotics. If you believe the bottleneck is reliability and unit economics in a specific vertical, then you build the simplest body that does the job, and you get to revenue three years earlier.

And I'd point out that the humanoid companies are quietly hedging. Look at how many "humanoids" are being deployed with wheeled bases, or with simplified grippers instead of dexterous hands. The form factor is converging toward something like "human upper body, whatever base works." That tells you the humanoid label is partly a marketing and fundraising decision. It's a story that's easy to tell investors and the public.

The thing I'd watch is who actually accumulates real-world interaction data fastest. The company that gets ten thousand robots doing useful work—even boring work—will have a data advantage that compounds, regardless of what shape those robots are. My suspicion is that the winners won't be the ones with the most human-looking robot. They'll be the ones who found a body that was good enough to deploy at scale early, and then let the model do the rest.

r001.rationale: The response mentions humanoids with wheeled bases and Agility’s legs, but does not suggest that the main hardware difference between company groups is simply whether robots have legs.

r002.rationale: It presents the view that because the world is built around human bodies, the human form is a natural universal fit for general-purpose robots.

astra-6.text:
I think the real question is what environment the robot needs to work in and what job it needs to do. If you’re operating in spaces designed for people, there’s a reasonable argument for a humanoid form: the tools, shelves, and workstations are already arranged around the human body. But that doesn’t automatically mean two legs are the best solution. If the floor is flat, wheels may be simpler and more reliable.

For a clearly defined task, a non-humanoid robot can be a better business. You can optimize the hardware around that task instead of paying for capabilities the customer doesn’t need. The humanoid bet is that a more general platform will eventually handle enough different tasks to justify the added complexity.

So I’d look less at how human the robot appears and more at how much useful work it can do, how often someone has to intervene, and what that work costs. A compelling demonstration is one thing. A machine that delivers value every day is another. That’s where these hardware bets will really be tested.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts two-legged robots with wheels, but frames the broader hardware bet as task-specific designs versus general-purpose platforms. It does not say that leg presence may be the main difference between humanoid-focused and other robotics companies.

r002.rationale: The response presents the argument that human-designed spaces favor humanoid form because tools, shelves, and workstations are arranged around people. It qualifies the case for two legs, but still communicates the view that human environments make humanoid form a natural fit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core question is whether you want to adapt the robot to the environment or adapt the environment to the robot. A lot of our environments are designed around people—stairs, doors, shelves, tools—so there’s a reasonable argument for a humanlike form. If you want one robot to work across many existing spaces, that compatibility matters.

But it doesn’t mean two legs and two arms are always the best engineering choice. If the task is moving things around a warehouse with a flat floor, wheels might be cheaper, more reliable, and more energy efficient. You shouldn’t take on the difficulty of walking unless walking gives you something you actually need.

So I’d look at the initial application. What work can the robot do, how often can it do it successfully, and at what cost? Humanoid companies are betting that a more general platform will eventually justify the extra complexity. Non-humanoid companies can optimize more directly for a particular job. Both can make sense, but the shape alone doesn’t tell you how useful the robot will be.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humanoid two-legged robots with wheeled robots, but it does not suggest that having legs may be the main hardware difference between humanoid-focused companies and other robotics companies.

r002.rationale: It says human-designed spaces make a humanlike form a reasonable option, but it does not present the stronger view that humanoids are necessarily the most natural fit.
